relations.note: Both rows are one computation, and each exists because a tool publishes a separate identifier for it: hashcat 32031 "Adobe AEM (SSPR, SHA-256 with Salt)" against hashcat 32030 "NetIQ SSPR (SHA-256 with Salt)". PROVEN RATHER THAN INFERRED, 2026-09-08: mdxfind pinned to ^SSPR-SHA256$ reproduced every member of this cluster from its OWN stored vector, against the local build RCS 1.579. A shared type name alone would not have established it -- mdxfind's EPISERVER reproduces a SHA-1 row and a SHA-256 row because the string carries a variant tag it dispatches on -- so the second control is that every digest in this cluster is 64 characters wide, which leaves the type no variant field to have read.

relations.note: AICH of a single block is SHA-1, and SHA1lsb35 is SHA-1 with the leading nibbles masked to zero, so any tool that ignores that field -- hashcat -m 100 skips positions 0-7 and john Raw-SHA1-Linkedin skips 0-4, measured 2026-09-01, and the mask is 5 nibbles wide -- reports one for the other. They agree on every input outside those nibbles and differ nowhere else that such a tool looks.

tool_note.hashcat: proven three ways because -m 100 alone is not enough: hashcat cracked this row's own vector under mode 100, john's Raw-SHA1 and dynamic_26 cracked it too with a FULL digest comparison, and Digest::SHA confirms sha1("password123") is cbfdac6008f9cab4083784cbd1874f76618d2a97 character for character. The third step is required here: measured 2026-08-31, hashcat -m 100 skips hash positions 0-7, so on its own it cannot tell this row from sha1lsb35, which is the same digest with those nibbles masked. discover-hashcat.pl's canary withheld the claim for exactly that reason; this is a human overriding it with the independent recomputation, not the tool's word.

tool_note.john: format discovered by round-trip search, not by name. Raw-SHA1-Linkedin was recorded here by discover-john.pl on 2026-08-31 and WITHDRAWN the same day. It is john's format for the LinkedIn leak, whose hashes have their leading nibbles zeroed, and it ignores hash positions 0-4 -- the 20 bits that leak zeroed -- measured position by position on 2026-09-01. That is the same defect the hashcat canary found in -m 100, at a different width: -m 100 skips 0-7. It therefore cracks any full SHA-1 digest as well, which is a collision and not a denotation. Raw-SHA1 and dynamic_26 both compare the whole digest and were re-checked position by position.

relations.note: hashcat 34000 "Argon2" accepts a SUPERSET of what 70000 "Argon2id [Bridged: reference implementation + tunings]" does. So the variant is read out of the string and 34000 spans the family. No split is owed.

tool_note.john: Round-tripped here on 2026-09-01, under both diskcryptor and diskcryptor-aes-opencl, against both vectors this entry carries. It had been tier upstream with a note blaming the ~819 candidate plaintexts harvested from john's source for not containing the answer; that diagnosis was wrong. john --list=format-details truncates example_ciphertext at 896 characters, so the header being attacked was never a loadable hash and no wordlist could have cracked it. relations.note: Measured 2026-09-04: the same computation, sha1($salt.$pass), stored two ways. Django writes sha1$<salt>$<digest> and mdxfind reads <digest>:<salt>, and this rows own vector reproduces under mdxfind pinned to SHA1SALTPASS once it is rewritten that way, handed to mdxfind with only the plaintext this row already states. No mdxfind type is named on this row because mdxfind cannot READ Djangos serialization; the type belongs to sha1-salt-pass, which is where a reader holding a bare <digest>:<salt> should land. hashcat tracks the two separately as modes 124 and 120.

entries.notes: Accepted 2026-09-04 from a name match that was then measured. TRANSCODE, proven: mdxfind's EPISERVER reader REFUSES base64 padding on the DIGEST field and accepts it on the salt. This entry's own vector reproduces under EPISERVER pinned with the single trailing '=' removed from the digest, handed to mdxfind with only the plaintext the john vector already states. That is why the 2026-09-03 sweep found this row's two siblings and not this row: their digests happen to be unpadded. The vector stored for mdxfind is mdxfind's own example rather than the transcode, because an independent credential is better evidence than the same one written twice.

relations.note: One computation, hashcat 7200 "GRUB 2" against hashcat 7100 "macOS v10.8+ (PBKDF2-SHA512)". tool_note.john: NOT REPRODUCED HERE, and CORRECTED 2026-09-06 about why. john publishes this identifier and a worked example, which is what tier `upstream` means. The earlier note on this row said the local round trip failed because john publishes no plaintext for its example and the plaintext was not in the ~819 candidates harvested from john's source. That is wrong, and it sends a reader looking for a wordlist that cannot help. The plaintext is G3RG3P00!, this row already stores it, and john recovers it on the first try. What john returns is G3RG3P0 -- seven characters -- and it says so itself: "Note: Passwords longer than 7 truncated (property of the hash)". nethalflm is a TRUNCATING format, so the strict byte comparison that gates a tier is not satisfied and should not be: the vector is upstream's and correct, the comparison is correct, and they answer different questions. This is NOT the case-insensitive-plaintext relaxation, which applies only where john says FMT_CASE is clear. Re-running seed-orphans.pl on this format will not change it.

These five john-named rows and their survivors are one computation, proven twice over: john's dynamic compiler recovers each loser's own plaintext from its own hash under the expression the survivor already carries at tier vector (gost($p), haval128_4($p), sha3_512($p), ripemd128($p), ripemd160($p)), and mdxfind pinned to ONE type reproduces BOTH rows' vectors on two different plaintexts. NOT the streebog-64-plain/gost2012-64 case, which stayed two rows under distinction naming: there the two rows carried two DIFFERENT mdxfind types, so each name had an identifier of its own. Here both rows carried the SAME type, and the loser was a strictly poorer view -- john's named format and nothing else, no hashcat mode, no hashpipe block -- so a reader arriving by john's label was landing on an incomplete answer. The label survives as an alias and as a john identifier on this row, and the tombstone redirects.

Both rows name mdxfind type GOST; this one at -i 2 and hash-gost-plain at -i 1. The iteration suffix is part of the identity (MD5x02 is john's dynamic_2, MD5x03 its dynamic_3), so these are two algorithms and not two names. Edge written 2026-09-07 from the data: same type, different iterations: is what `iterates` means, and no judgment was involved.

entries.notes: The plaintext here was DERIVED by search on 2026-08-31 -- john publishes an example ciphertext and no plaintext, so seed-orphans.pl hands john the example and candidates harvested from john's own source and takes back whatever falls. That is sound only where john's comparison is exact, and this format is one john flags FMT_NOT_EXACT: --list=format-all-details prints "Collisions possible (as in likely) yes" and a run prints "Note: This format may emit false positives". The candidate list is harvested from the same test arrays that carry the collisions, so the search returned one. john's own test array states BOTH strings for this ciphertext and labels them: {"$adxcrypt$54886955", "99999999"} // default credentials, and {"$adxcrypt$54886955", "786r"} // collided password, works fine on a real system. This entry carried the collision. Corrected 2026-09-04 to the default credential, re-run under john and recovered. The mdxfind absence on this row was measured on 2026-09-03 against the previous plaintext. hashpipe was re-asked with the corrected pair on 2026-09-04 and still names no type, which is the half of that verdict a plaintext can change. A full-inventory mdxfind re-run against the corrected pairs found nothing in 900 seconds but was cut off at that cap, so it is consistent with the verdict rather than a fresh proof of it.

entries.expr_note: mdxfind type LEET-SHA512-WRL-USER (e444) is MULTI-EMIT: it computes several candidate digests per input and matches if any one reproduces the stored hash. There is therefore no single expression to record, and writing one of the emitted forms into expression: would be a false claim even though the string itself is correct. This is also why two vectors of such a type can disagree with each other, and why a tool matching one of them is not evidence about the other.

entries.expr_note: mdxfind type MD4UTF16MD5HUM (e575) is MULTI-EMIT: it computes several candidate digests per input and matches if any one reproduces the stored hash. This is also why two vectors of such a type can disagree with each other, and why a tool matching one of them is not evidence about the other.

entries.expr_note: mdxfind type MD4UTF16SHA1HUM (e576) is MULTI-EMIT: it computes several candidate digests per input and matches if any one reproduces the stored hash. There is therefore no single expression to record, and writing one of the emitted forms into expression: would be a false claim even though the string itself is correct. This is also why two vectors of such a type can disagree with each other, and why a tool matching one of them is not evidence about the other.

entries.expr_note: WITHDRAWN 2026-09-02. This row carried md5(base64(md5_raw(md5($p)))) at tier upstream, transcribed from hx Appendix A for e243, and triage recorded it as reproducing 1 of 2 vectors. Both vectors are correct and the expression was the false claim: mdxfind type MD5BASE64MD5RAWMD5 is MULTI-EMIT, so no single expression describes it. mdxfind.c b64md5raw computes md5 of the whole 24-character base64 into mdcur[0] and, under if (len > 18), md5 of the same base64 minus its last two characters into mdcur[1], then checkhash()es both. mdxfind -z counts 2 emissions for this type, RCS 1.545, measured 2026-09-02. mdxfind own hx VM reproduces this row first vector from the padded form and its second from the 22-character form, so the two vectors corroborate the type rather than contradicting each other.

entries.name: md5(cap(md5($plain)).":".$username)
entries.notes: This row is mdxfind type MD5CAPMD5USER. CORRECTED TWICE on 2026-08-31, and the second correction matters more than the first. Waffle named the unknown vector d4f7dec5...:abc123 as the colon form, confirmed here by independent Digest::MD5 and by local mdxfind pinned to ^MD5CAPMD5USER$ with -F. But the hx specification (rev 1.15) Appendix A Note [24] then showed the stronger fact: MD5CAPMD5USER is a MULTI-EMIT type. It emits BOTH md5(cap(md5($p)).$u) and md5(cap(md5($p)).":".$u) and matches if either reproduces the stored digest. So this row is not one computation, and neither of its two vectors is anomalous -- 05b56c69... is the colonless emit and d4f7dec5... is the colon emit. The first correction here wrongly called the colonless vector foreign and removed it; it is restored. A copy also sits on md5-md5-pass-salt, which is the row for the colonless construction in its own right. john has no format for either emit: discover-john.pl ran all 957 formats against the colon vector with zero matches, and the dynamic language has no literal-string token. The 198,534-construction sweep that failed to identify this missed it because it enumerated terms and never a literal separator.

relations.note: MD5MD5USER and MD5CAPMD5USER differ only by cap() on the inner hex digest, which is a no-op whenever that digest starts with a digit. md5('rosetta') is 975790df..., so both types reproduce this shared vector identically; they diverge on any plaintext whose md5 starts with a letter.

entries.notes: This row is mdxfind type MD5MD5USER. CORRECTED TWICE on 2026-08-31, and the second correction matters more than the first. Waffle named the unknown vector d4f7dec5...:abc123 as the colon form, confirmed here by independent Digest::MD5 and by local mdxfind pinned to ^MD5MD5USER$ with -F. But the hx specification (rev 1.15) Appendix A Note [24] then showed the stronger fact: MD5MD5USER is a MULTI-EMIT type. It emits BOTH md5(md5($p).$u) and md5(md5($p).":".$u) and matches if either reproduces the stored digest. So this row is not one computation, and neither of its two vectors is anomalous -- 05b56c69... is the colonless emit and d4f7dec5... is the colon emit. The first correction here wrongly called the colonless vector foreign and removed it; it is restored. A copy also sits on md5-md5-pass-salt, which is the row for the colonless construction in its own right. john has no format for either emit: discover-john.pl ran all 957 formats against the colon vector with zero matches, and the dynamic language has no literal-string token. The 198,534-construction sweep that failed to identify this missed it because it enumerated terms and never a literal separator.

relations.note: MD5MD5USER and MD5CAPMD5USER differ only by cap() on the inner hex digest, which is a no-op whenever that digest starts with a digit. md5('rosetta') is 975790df..., so both types reproduce this shared vector identically; they diverge on any plaintext whose md5 starts with a letter.

entries.expr_note: mdxfind type MD5MD5PASS (e123) is MULTI-EMIT: it computes several candidate digests per input and matches if any one reproduces the stored hash. There is therefore no single expression to record, and writing one of the emitted forms into expression: would be a false claim even though the string itself is correct. This is also why two vectors of such a type can disagree with each other, and why a tool matching one of them is not evidence about the other.

entries.expr_note: the construction upstream states for mdxfind type MD5-MD5MD5PASSSALT-PEP (e819) uses a PEPPER: a site-wide secret that appears in no hash and cannot be derived from one. hx makes it a built-in variable beside pass, salt and salt2, with its own slot in the VM, and mdxfind reads it from a file (-j global array, -P per-type). john's dynamic expression language has no equivalent: $s2 is a second PER-HASH salt, not a site secret, and a $c1 constant would have to carry the value, which is exactly what a pepper does not publish. The absence therefore holds for every possible pepper rather than for this vector, which is what makes it a lookup. It says nothing about whether john can CRACK this. Established from mdxfind's source (hx.y line 19, hx_vm.c HX_SLOT_PEPPER) on 2026-09-02.

entries.expr_note: Established from mdxfind's own source and a measurement, not from a document: Appendix A writes only the prose "(complex: iterates over single-char salts)" for this family and Note [24] does not name it. mdxfind.c sweeps a single salt byte over 9 and 32..126 -- 96 values -- and emits five placements at each (s.d, d.s, s.d.s, s.s.d and d.s.s, where d is the hex inner digest); "mdxfind -z" prints 480 candidates per password, which is 5 x 96. Measured 2026-09-02 against RCS 1.545. The name and aliases on this entry are those five placements. mdxfind type MD51SALTMD5MD5MD5 (e343) is MULTI-EMIT: it computes several candidate digests per input and matches if any one reproduces the stored hash. There is therefore no single expression to record, and writing one of the emitted forms into expression: would be a false claim even though the string itself is correct. This is also why two vectors of such a type can disagree with each other, and why a tool matching one of them is not evidence about the other.

tool_note.mdxfind: `iterations` was corrected from 2 to 1 on 2026-09-05. The vector is right and was never in doubt; the DEPTH LABEL was wrong, inherited from a binary that reported the base one round early. mdxfind revision 1.290 (2026-04-09) regressed the RAW family -- "the base was reported one round early, so x01 became X(pass) instead of X(X_bin(pass))" -- and revision 1.549 (2026-08-30) restored it. Measured 2026-09-05: this entry's own stored vector reproduces under mdxfind RCS 1.576 at x01, and `hashpipe -c` pinned to the same type independently reports x01. It reproduced at x02 only under the regressed RCS 1.545, which is where the 2 came from. Note what this ALSO settles: hashpipe's john_map.h has published x01 for these types all along, and data/upstream-disagreements.yaml recorded that as an "iteration-numbering" convention difference. It was not a convention difference; it was this bug, and upstream's map was right.

entries.expr_note: WITHDRAWN 2026-09-02: this entry read cap(md5($p)), transcribed from the hx specification's Appendix A for mdxfind type MD5CAP (e353). That string is wrong twice over, and Appendix A is wrong about this type in the same way CLAUDE.md already records for e308. mdxfind.c JOB_MD5CAP capitalizes mdbuf[0] ONLY (if (islower(mdbuf[0]))), where hx's bare cap() moves the first lower-case LETTER anywhere; and its loop is for (x = 2; x <= Maxiter; x++) with checkhash INSIDE, so the type never emits a one-iteration value -- mdxfind -i 1 pinned to this type matches nothing. The replacement was established three independent ways, all agreeing on this entry's own vector: the source, the binary reporting it as MD5CAPx02 at -i 2, and hx evaluating md5(cap(md5(pass), 0)). Stays tier upstream because john's dynamic language has no cap() token, so no round-trip can ever promote it. The other twelve cap() entries are NOT affected: five of them carry vectors that discriminate between the two readings and all five match hx's bare cap(), so e353 is an outlier rather than a family error.; TRIAGE 2026-09-08 [corroborated]: no john format, so john ships no control vectors; but RosettaExpr -- an implementation independent of all three crackers -- computes this expression over the entry's own vector(s) and reproduces 1 of 1. That is corroboration, not tier vector, which needs john's own compiler
entries.name: MD5CAP

relations.note: MD5CAP is md5(cap(md5($p),0)) and its cap() touches position 0 only, so whenever the inner digest does not START with a lower-case letter the type is byte-identical to two-iteration plain MD5 -- which is how john's dynamic_2 and plain MD5 crack its vector without denoting it. Corrected 2026-09-02 from a note that described hx's bare cap() (first lower-case letter anywhere), a different function that this type does not use.

entries.notes: The vector is hashpipe's published example, verified under hashpipe -c pinned to MD5DSALT, and mdxfind will not read it back, so the mdxfind mapping stays at tier `asserted`. Measured 2026-09-04: pinned with -h '^MD5DSALT$', mdxfind performs ZERO hash calculations on the line under -f and zero under -F, at every iteration count tried, so it is declining the input shape rather than computing and missing. hashpipe's verify_md5dsalt parses the line as a 32-hex digest, a colon, and a salt of 2 to 6 characters, then sweeps the ways that salt can be split -- this is one of the multi-emit DSALT types CLAUDE.md records, which is why no single expression belongs on this row either.

entries.expr_note: mdxfind type MD5MD5HUM (e363) is MULTI-EMIT: it computes several candidate digests per input and matches if any one reproduces the stored hash. entries.name: MD5SPECAM
entries.notes: mdxfind and hashpipe do NOT compute the same thing under this name, measured 2026-09-04, and the vector on this row is hashpipe's. hashpipe's compute_md5specam is md5($p . md5_raw($p)) -- it takes neither salt nor user (it is registered with flags 0 and casts both away) -- and its published example 9018942a51656d6055f0c20024dd4f48:password123 was confirmed three independent ways: hashpipe -c pinned to MD5SPECAM, the source itself, and a recomputation in Perl. mdxfind's JOB_MD5SPECAM (mdxfind.c, the case at ~27795) reads a USERID off the line, lower-casing it up to the first colon, and breaks out when that field is empty -- it is a member of the AM family, whose sibling MD5AM hashpipe's own source records as md5(user . "::" . lower($p)). Pinned with -h '^MD5SPECAM$', mdxfind performs ZERO hash calculations on this line under -f and zero again under -F with a userid field appended, so it is declining the input shape rather than computing and missing. The mdxfind mapping therefore stays at tier `asserted`: what is on this row is proven for hashpipe's MD5SPECAM and says nothing yet about mdxfind's.

entries.expr_note: mdxfind type MD5UCBASE64MD5RAW (e375) is MULTI-EMIT: it computes several candidate digests per input and matches if any one reproduces the stored hash. There is therefore no single expression to record, and writing one of the emitted forms into expression: would be a false claim even though the string itself is correct. This is also why two vectors of such a type can disagree with each other, and why a tool matching one of them is not evidence about the other.

entries.notes: The vendored catalog renders this type's example digest in uppercase hex, and mdxfind will not read it back in that case, so the seeding pass could not verify it. mdxfind -z computes the same digest in lowercase for the same plaintext, and pinned to ^MD5UCBASE64SHA1RAW$ it reproduces that form; the stored vector is the catalog's own digest re-cased, not one we invented. Fourteen other types carry an uppercase example (MD5UC, SHA1UC, SHA256UC, RACF, ORACLE7 among them) and are NOT all the same story -- MD5UC and SHA256UC do not reproduce in either case.

entries.name: MS Office 2016 - SheetProtection
entries.notes:
WHERE THE HASH LIVES. This is not document encryption and office2john does
not extract it. An .xlsx is a zip; the digest is a cleartext attribute run
on the protection element of the relevant part:

    <sheetProtection algorithmName="SHA-512" hashValue="..."
                     saltValue="..." spinCount="100000" sheet="1"/>

THE ATTRIBUTE NAMES ARE NOT UNIFORM, which is where a naive extractor goes
wrong. `<sheetProtection>`, `<chartsheetProtection>` and `<fileSharing>` use
the bare names above. `<workbookProtection>` carries TWO INDEPENDENT digests
under PREFIXED names: workbookAlgorithmName / workbookHashValue /
workbookSaltValue / workbookSpinCount for the structure password, and
revisionsAlgorithmName / revisionsHashValue / revisionsSaltValue /
revisionsSpinCount for the revisions password. Word's
`<w:documentProtection>`, `<w:writeProtection>` and `<w:modifyVerifier>` use
the bare names again, namespace-prefixed.

Measured 2026-09-03: sheetProtection, fileSharing and BOTH prefixed
workbookProtection slots round-trip at mode 25300, against fixtures whose
attribute spellings come from openpyxl's own schema classes rather than from
recollection. The Word elements were exercised only against a hand-written
.docx, so those spellings remain spec reading and not measurement.

THE HASHCAT LINE is built from three of those attributes and two literals:

    $office$2016$0$<spinCount>$<saltValue>$<hashValue>

`2016` and `0` never vary; salt precedes hash; both go in base64 exactly as
the XML spells them. Getting the order wrong or using ':' as the separator
produces hashcat's "separator unmatched", which reads like a corrupt hash
rather than a malformed line.

HASHCAT'S PARSER IS STRICTER THAN THE FILE FORMAT, and its error names the
wrong field. src/modules/module_25300.c in v7.1.2-549 requires the spinCount
token to be six digits AND to equal 100000 (line 165), the salt to be
exactly 24 base64 characters decoding to 16 bytes, and the digest exactly 88
decoding to 64. Probed against the binary across ten spin values on
2026-09-03: only 100000 loads, and every other value is rejected as
"Salt-value exception", which sends the reader off to inspect the salt.
Excel's own default is 100000 so most real files pass, but a document
written with any other spin count has a real, well-formed SHA-512 digest and
NO hashcat mode at all.

THE CONSTRUCTION, measured 2026-09-03 by reproducing hashcat's own example
vector above with all four plausible orderings and finding exactly one
match:

    H_0 = SHA512(saltValue . utf16le(password))
    H_i = SHA512(H_{i-1} . uint32le(i-1))   for i = 1 .. spinCount
    hashValue = base64(H_spinCount)

The counter is APPENDED and 0-BASED. Agile ENCRYPTION prepends it, and that
difference is the whole trap: the prepending order computes a perfectly
well-formed digest that simply is not this one, with nothing to indicate the
error. It is SHA-512 throughout, not SHA-256; secondary write-ups say SHA-256
and are wrong. hashcat's 25300 kernel is SHA-512 only, so a file whose
algorithmName is anything else has no mode.

Proven end to end on 2026-09-03 against a synthesized .xlsx carrying a
SHA-512 sheetProtection element for a known password, extracted from the
XML and cracked by hashcat at this mode.

The pre-2013 form of the same feature is a 16-bit verifier in a `password`
attribute, which is a different algorithm and has its own entry:
ms-office-sheetprotection-legacy. And for either form, note that the file is
not encrypted -- deleting the protection element and rezipping opens the
sheet, so cracking is only warranted when the password itself is the object.

entries.application: Microsoft Excel <=2010 file format; still written by openpyxl and by LibreOffice
entries.denotation: Binary Document Password Verifier Derivation Method 1
entries.expr_note: the construction is a 15-bit rotate-and-xor over the password read BACKWARDS, then an xor of the length and of the constant 0xCE4B. john's dynamic expression vocabulary has no rotate, no xor and no reversal, so this cannot be written as an expression at all -- that is a lookup against the function names in john's own --list=subformats, not an opinion. It is also separate from whether john can CRACK it, and john cannot: see tools.john.
entries.name: MS Office SheetProtection - legacy 16-bit verifier
entries.notes:
A 16-bit password verifier, not a hash in any useful sense. In an OOXML part
it appears under a DIFFERENT ATTRIBUTE NAME on each element: `password` on
`<sheetProtection>` and `<chartsheetProtection>`, `workbookPassword` and
`revisionsPassword` on `<workbookProtection>` (two independent passwords on
one element), and `reservationPassword` on `<fileSharing>`. Spellings taken
from openpyxl's schema classes and exercised 2026-09-03. It is also the data
of the BIFF PASSWORD and PROTECT records in a pre-2007 .xls. The native form
-- the one the vector
above is written in -- is FOUR HEXADECIMAL DIGITS exactly as the attribute
spells them, with no wrapper, no salt and no iteration count, because there
is nowhere for any of those to go.

The algorithm, from MS-OFFCRYPTO 2.3.7.1: start at 0; for each character of
the password taken from LAST to FIRST, rotate the running value left within
15 bits and xor the character code; then rotate once more, xor the password
length, and xor the constant 0xCE4B. Reimplemented and measured 2026-09-03
against the value openpyxl 3.0.9 writes for "P@ssw0rd", which is the vector
above.

BYTE ORDER IS A TRAP. The XML attribute and the BIFF record render the same
word in opposite orders, so published write-ups give "AB94" for the value
this repository records as "94AB". They are the same verifier. Check which
container a quoted value came out of before comparing it to anything.

THE ORIGINAL PASSWORD IS NOT RECOVERABLE and no tool will ever make it so:
16 bits cannot carry it. What is recoverable is a COLLIDING password, which
unlocks the sheet just as well. Measured 2026-09-03: 'DbOUJLIb' verifies to
94AB, found in 24065 random 8-character tries in under a second. Do not
report such a string as the password.

Collisions are dense but NOT uniformly reachable, which is the practical
gotcha. Exhausting printable ASCII at lengths 1 to 4 -- 82,317,120 strings
-- reaches only 1536 distinct verifier values out of 65536, and 94AB is not
among them, because a short password is rotated too few times for the high
bits ever to be set. Search at the same length as the original or longer; a
short-candidate sweep can return nothing and prove nothing.

Operationally, cracking is usually the wrong move for either form of sheet
protection. The file is not encrypted: deleting the protection element and
rezipping opens the sheet, and only a genuine interest in the password
itself (credential reuse, an investigation) justifies the rest.

entries.name: NETLMv2
entries.notes: Created 2026-09-06 by splitting netntlmv2, which was holding two computations -- something CLAUDE.md forbids and that row's own notes had already flagged and left to a curator. The split is a measurement, not a reading of the names: handed to john NATIVELY, one vector at a time, netntlmv2 cracks the other three vectors of that row and REFUSES this one, while netlmv2 cracks this one and refuses those three. Each format declines to load the other's string, so the two are not alternative spellings. This vector is john's own published example and is the short one -- an 8-byte blob, far short of an NTLMv2 one, which is what made it visible in the first place. NETLMv2 is john-only: no hashcat mode, mdxfind type or hashpipe type carries the name. NOTE FOR ANYONE VERIFYING THIS ROW: verify-vectors.pl cannot check it. It writes a synthetic login and a TAB before each hash, which is right for a hash that is only a digest and wrong here, because a NETLMv2 ciphertext EMBEDS its own login and john will not parse it once that field has been displaced. Hand it to john natively. CORRECTED 2026-09-07: the sentence above says NETLMv2 is john-only because no hashcat mode, mdxfind type or hashpipe type CARRIES THE NAME. That is still true and it is about names. It must not be read as a claim about capability, which the lean chunk-1 sweep of that date measured to be false: mdxfind pinned to NETNTLMV2 reproduces this row's vector. See the mdxfind block for what that identifier does and does not establish. The name veto in absence.pl is exactly this shape of blind spot, and it is why an absence was never published here.

tool_note.john: Round-tripped NATIVELY, one vector per invocation: format(s) netlmv2 could not parse this entry's vectors under the grouped scheme this tool normally uses, which writes a synthetic login and a TAB before every hash. This ciphertext EMBEDS its own login, so displacing that field is what breaks the parse -- john loaded nothing, which is not the same as cracking nothing, and its own --show summary is what said so. The stored vector is unchanged and is exactly what john was handed. Reproduce it with: john --format=<label> --wordlist=<one candidate> <one hash>, with no --field-separator-char.
tool_note.mdxfind: Found by the lean chunk-1 mdxfind sweep of 2026-09-07 and round-tripped pinned. WHAT THE IDENTIFIER DOES AND DOES NOT SAY: mdxfind has no NETLMV2 type -- its only neighbours are e897 NETNTLMV1 and e898 NETNTLMV2 -- and NETNTLMV2 pinned reproduces ALL FOUR vectors across this entry and netntlmv2, which is the pair john needs TWO formats for. That is the family, not a fluke: LMv2 and NTLMv2 responses are the same HMAC-MD5 construction over a blob, and mdxfind takes the blob as given where john's two parsers do not. The negative control is NETNTLMV1, which refuses all four in the same run. So this is a real mapping for a reader holding an LMv2 response -- and it is NOT a discriminator: pinned to NETNTLMV2, mdxfind cannot tell this row from netntlmv2 the way john's netlmv2 and netntlmv2 can, each of which refuses the other's string. Whether the two rows therefore want a relation is a curator's call and has not been made.

entries.notes: john reads BOTH tools' NTLMv2 serializations: measured 2026-09-01, netntlmv2 and ntlmv2-opencl load and crack this entry's hashcat-form vectors (USER::DOMAIN:challenge:response:blob) unchanged. An earlier run of this session reported "No password hashes loaded" and three re-serialized vectors were briefly added on that basis; the cause was a --field-separator-char=tab passed by the probing tool, which governs how john splits LOGIN from HASH when READING a file, so a tab made john treat each whole line as one login. The vectors were withdrawn and the tool fixed. Kerberos AS-REP is NOT like this: john genuinely cannot read hashcat's $krb5asrep$ field order, which is why those rows do carry a transcoded vector. Two reasons this block is still tier asserted, neither of which is doubt about NETNTLMv2 itself. (1) It names netlmv2, a DIFFERENT computation, and a block carries one tier for every identifier in it; netlmv2 recovers none of these vectors, and the fourth vector (aTest:::...:A1E7281FE8C10E53, an 8-byte blob far short of an NTLMv2 one) looks like the NETLMv2 one. That is a row holding two computations, which CLAUDE.md forbids, and splitting it is curation. (2) verify-vectors.pl cannot check this format at all: it writes a synthetic login and a TAB before each hash, which is right for a hash that is only a digest and wrong here, because a NETNTLMv2 ciphertext EMBEDS its own login (USER::DOMAIN:...) and john will not parse it once that field has been displaced. Measured 2026-09-01: the same vectors load and crack under netntlmv2 and ntlmv2-opencl when handed to john natively, 3 of 4, and verify-vectors.pl reports 0 of 4 for all three identifiers. SPLIT 2026-09-06. netlmv2 and the aTest::: vector moved to their own row, lmv2-c-r. This resolves reason (1) in the paragraph above, which had been recorded here since 2026-09-01 and left to a curator: the row was holding two computations. The split was measured rather than read off the names -- handed to john natively, one vector at a time, netntlmv2 cracks the three vectors still here and REFUSES the aTest one, while netlmv2 cracks the aTest one and refuses these three, each declining to LOAD the other's string. Reason (2) stands unchanged and always will: verify-vectors.pl cannot check a challenge-response format at all, because it displaces the login field this ciphertext embeds, so this block is verified by hand or not at all.

entries.notes: The plaintext here was DERIVED by search on 2026-08-31 -- john publishes an example ciphertext and no plaintext, so seed-orphans.pl hands john the example and candidates harvested from john's own source and takes back whatever falls. That is sound only where john's comparison is exact, and this format is one john flags FMT_NOT_EXACT: --list=format-all-details prints "Collisions possible (as in likely) yes" and a run prints "Note: This format may emit false positives". The candidate list is harvested from the same test arrays that carry the collisions, so the search returned one. john's source states "password" for this ciphertext. The search returned the 16-character literal string \xc0\xc1\xc2\xc3, which is a second defect in the same harvest: it reads a C string literal without unescaping it, so the backslashes become part of the candidate. Corrected 2026-09-04, re-run under john and recovered. The mdxfind absence on this row was measured on 2026-09-03 against the previous plaintext. hashpipe was re-asked with the corrected pair on 2026-09-04 and still names no type, which is the half of that verdict a plaintext can change. A full-inventory mdxfind re-run against the corrected pairs found nothing in 900 seconds but was cut off at that cap, so it is consistent with the verdict rather than a fresh proof of it.

entries.notes: Vector 'john' added 2026-09-06: the SAME credential as this row's first vector, re-serialized into the form john's osc format reads. It is not independent evidence -- do not read two agreeing vectors here as corroboration. The two spellings differ in ORDER and in ENCODING: this row stores <hash>:<salt> with the salt as text, and osc wants $OSC$<salt as hex>$<hash>, so the salt 'ab' becomes 6162. Measured 2026-09-06: handed the colon form, osc answers "No password hashes loaded", while the four dynamics on this row read it unchanged. The re-encoding was not assumed: the $OSC$ string was handed to john with only the plaintext the stored vector already states, and fell.

relations.note: Both rows are one computation, and each exists because a tool publishes a separate identifier for it: hashcat 20 "md5($salt.$pass)" against hashcat 21 "osCommerce, xt:Commerce". PROVEN RATHER THAN INFERRED, 2026-09-08: mdxfind pinned to ^MD5SALTPASS$ reproduced every member of this cluster from its OWN stored vector, against the local build RCS 1.579. relations.note: merged 2026-09-01: one computation under two names, proven by john's dynamic compiler against both vectors. Royce chose the john-named row on 2026-09-01: panama-johnpanama carries john's Panama format, and dynamic_320 now sits beside it so a reader arriving by either name lands here

Both rows name mdxfind type PANAMA; this one at -i 2 and panama-johnpanama at -i 1. The iteration suffix is part of the identity (MD5x02 is john's dynamic_2, MD5x03 its dynamic_3), so these are two algorithms and not two names. Edge written 2026-09-07 from the data: same type, different iterations: is what `iterates` means, and no judgment was involved.

entries.name: PARALLEL
entries.notes: No vector exists to seed, measured 2026-09-04, and this is the one type in the inventory for which that is a fact about the tools rather than a gap in this repository. hashpipe registers PARALLEL with no ht->example at all, so `hashpipe -T` skips it -- it is one of the two skipped types the generated data/tools/hashpipe.yaml header names -- and `hashpipe -G`, which generates a vector for a type that has none, emits nothing for it either because it has no compute function and no chain to drive. mdxfind's own inventory row (e426) carries no example_vector, and e426 is the single index mdxfind has that hashpipe does not. Nothing here can move until one of the two tools publishes a vector.

tool_note.mdxfind: PARALLEL is not a hash. mdxfind's maintainer describes it as a measurement tool rather than an algorithm, and it emits nothing: measured 2026-09-04, run pinned with -M under -z alone, with -s and with -u, stdout empty in every case. So this entry can never reach tier vector and the absence of a vector is a property of the type, not a gap in this repository. The identifier itself is real -- it is in mdxfind's own type table -- and that is all the mapping claims.

relations.note: One computation, hashcat 32050 "NetIQ SSPR (PBKDF2WithHmacSHA1)" against hashcat 12000 "PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA1". PROVEN, not inferred from the shared type name: mdxfind pinned to ^PBKDF2-SHA1$ reproduced BOTH rows from their own stored vectors, one invocation per row with one hash and one candidate, against the local build RCS 1.579 on 2026-09-08. The solo shape is not a convenience -- a grouped run attributes by matching the echoed hash string, and mdxfind RE-SERIALIZES these: it returns grub-2's "grub.pbkdf2.sha512.1024.<salt>.<digest>" as "$ml$1024$...", and the SSPR and passlib rows as "sha256:<iter>:<b64 salt>:<b64 digest>". An earlier grouped test reported four of these rows as NOT reproduced for that reason alone, and every one of them was already at tier vector with mdxfind in its reads_in. The two rows differ in the KDF's PARAMETERS -- iteration count, output length, and for scrypt N/r/p -- which are carried inside the hash string. Royce decided 2026-09-08 that those are INPUTS like a salt rather than part of the computation, which is why one mdxfind type reads every member of this cluster, and which follows the md5($s.$p) cluster already committed with four rows whose salts differ freely.

relations.note: One computation, hashcat 32060 "NetIQ SSPR (PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256)" against hashcat 10000 "Django (PBKDF2-SHA256)". PROVEN, not inferred from the shared type name: mdxfind pinned to ^PBKDF2-SHA256$ reproduced BOTH rows from their own stored vectors, one invocation per row with one hash and one candidate, against the local build RCS 1.579 on 2026-09-08. The solo shape is not a convenience -- a grouped run attributes by matching the echoed hash string, and mdxfind RE-SERIALIZES these: it returns grub-2's "grub.pbkdf2.sha512.1024.<salt>.<digest>" as "$ml$1024$...", and the SSPR and passlib rows as "sha256:<iter>:<b64 salt>:<b64 digest>". An earlier grouped test reported four of these rows as NOT reproduced for that reason alone, and every one of them was already at tier vector with mdxfind in its reads_in. The two rows differ in the KDF's PARAMETERS -- iteration count, output length, and for scrypt N/r/p -- which are carried inside the hash string. Royce decided 2026-09-08 that those are INPUTS like a salt rather than part of the computation, which is why one mdxfind type reads every member of this cluster, and which follows the md5($s.$p) cluster already committed with four rows whose salts differ freely.

entries.expr_note: CORRECTED 2026-09-02. This row previously carried sha1(utf16be(upper($p))), transcribed from the hx specification Appendix A entry for mdxfind type PEOPLESOFT (e858). Appendix A is wrong TWICE there: the encoding is UTF-16LE, not BE, and there is no upper() at all. mdxfind SOURCE settles it and outranks the document -- mdxfind.c JOB_PEOPLESOFT (line 20644) converts the candidate through iconv descriptor cd, opened UTF-8 to UTF-16LE//IGNORE at line 11690, then mysha1() then b64_encode() of 20 bytes, with no case folding anywhere. Corroborated four further ways, all 2026-09-02: mdxfind own hx VM, built -DHX_STANDALONE from the same tree, evaluates base64(sha1_bin(utf16le(pass))) to this row own vector byte for byte INCLUDING the = padding; an independent Perl recomputation (Digest::SHA + MIME::Base64) reproduces it and reproduces NEITHER of Appendix A two errors; hashcat -m 133 already round-trips this vector; and john dynamic compiler cracks the same digest under dynamic=sha1_64(utf16($p)). The tier stays upstream and not vector because john _64 flavor emits UNPADDED base64, so john was handed lACuKESOE2QXTd4mmyzOG8qdfug with the trailing = stripped -- a transcode of the stored ciphertext, not this row own hash, and mdxfind loader requires that padding (len == 28 and line[27] == = at mdxfind.c line 43971). Anyone running the john_dynamic_expr on the stored vector must strip the = first or john will not load it.; TRIAGE 2026-09-08 [corroborated]: no john format, so john ships no control vectors; but RosettaExpr -- an implementation independent of all three crackers -- computes this expression over the entry's own vector(s) and reproduces 1 of 1. That is corroboration, not tier vector, which needs john's own compiler

relations.note: One computation, hashcat 32060 "NetIQ SSPR (PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256)" against hashcat 20300 "Python passlib pbkdf2-sha256". That the vector was IN the search is not assumed -- the same sweep reported a hit on another vector of the same shape, a positive control measured in the same run by the same binary, and without it finding nothing would not be evidence. Every applicable type ran to completion; a type killed at the timeout is counted as untested and withholds this verdict. No mdxfind type name matches any identifier this entry publishes either, normalized by the separator-drift rule. entries.notes: Created 2026-09-04. This corpus had no row for plain SHA-1 as such, which is what blocked resolving the two-computations problem on sha1-substr-0-32: john's Raw-SHA1 sits on aich, sha1uc and netscape-ldap, and the truncation row held mdxfind's SHA1, so deleting the plain-SHA-1 claims there would have stranded them rather than rehomed them. They are rehomed here.

relations.note: Both rows name mdxfind type SHA1; this one at -i 2 and sha1 at -i 1. The iteration suffix is part of the identity (MD5x02 is john's dynamic_2, MD5x03 its dynamic_3), so these are two algorithms and not two names. Edge written 2026-09-07 from the data: same type, different iterations: is what `iterates` means, and no judgment was involved.

Both rows name mdxfind type SHA1; this one at -i 3 and sha1 at -i 1. The iteration suffix is part of the identity (MD5x02 is john's dynamic_2, MD5x03 its dynamic_3), so these are two algorithms and not two names. Edge written 2026-09-07 from the data: same type, different iterations: is what `iterates` means, and no judgment was involved.

sha1-substr-0-32 is this computation cut to its first 32 hex characters. Split out of that row on 2026-09-04 by Royce's decision: it was carrying both, and only john's dynamic_1023 truncates. Every identifier here computes plain SHA-1 and no cut, and every one of them was round-tripped against this vector before the split -- nothing was re-tiered by moving it. mdxfind reproduces this row under BOTH SHA1 (e8) and AICH (e21), pinned, through its generic truncated matching at a comparison width of 32. NO mdxfind mapping is recorded: decided by Royce 2026-09-07 that finding a row is not denoting it. MD5 was pinned in the same run and REFUSED, which is the control that says the match is about these types and not about mdxfind reading a short digest loosely.

entries.expr_note: Established from mdxfind's own source and a measurement, not from a document: Appendix A writes only the prose "(complex: iterates over single-char salts)" for this family and Note [24] does not name it. mdxfind.c sweeps a single salt byte over 9 and 32..126 -- 96 values -- and emits five placements at each (s.d, d.s, s.d.s, s.s.d and d.s.s, where d is the hex inner digest); "mdxfind -z" prints 480 candidates per password, which is 5 x 96. Measured 2026-09-02 against RCS 1.545. The name and aliases on this entry are those five placements. mdxfind type SHA11SALTMD5 (e311) is MULTI-EMIT: it computes several candidate digests per input and matches if any one reproduces the stored hash. There is therefore no single expression to record, and writing one of the emitted forms into expression: would be a false claim even though the string itself is correct. This is also why two vectors of such a type can disagree with each other, and why a tool matching one of them is not evidence about the other.

tool_note.mdxfind: MYSQL5MD5 added 2026-08-31 by seed-orphans.pl: mdxfind names it "MYSQL5MD5", which is this entry's own expression, and mdxfind at that identifier recovers this entry's own vector. It had no entry at all before. `iterations` was corrected from 2 to 1 on 2026-09-05. The vector is right and was never in doubt; the DEPTH LABEL was wrong, inherited from a binary that reported the base one round early. mdxfind revision 1.290 (2026-04-09) regressed the RAW family -- "the base was reported one round early, so x01 became X(pass) instead of X(X_bin(pass))" -- and revision 1.549 (2026-08-30) restored it. Measured 2026-09-05: this entry's own stored vector reproduces under mdxfind RCS 1.576 at x01, and `hashpipe -c` pinned to the same type independently reports x01. It reproduced at x02 only under the regressed RCS 1.545, which is where the 2 came from. Note what this ALSO settles: hashpipe's john_map.h has published x01 for these types all along, and data/upstream-disagreements.yaml recorded that as an "iteration-numbering" convention difference. It was not a convention difference; it was this bug, and upstream's map was right.

entries.expr_note: the construction upstream states for mdxfind type SHA1-MD5CAPPEPPER-MD5SALT (e654) uses a PEPPER: a site-wide secret that appears in no hash and cannot be derived from one. hx makes it a built-in variable beside pass, salt and salt2, with its own slot in the VM, and mdxfind reads it from a file (-j global array, -P per-type). john's dynamic expression language has no equivalent: $s2 is a second PER-HASH salt, not a site secret, and a $c1 constant would have to carry the value, which is exactly what a pepper does not publish. The absence therefore holds for every possible pepper rather than for this vector, which is what makes it a lookup. It says nothing about whether john can CRACK this. Established from mdxfind's source (hx.y line 19, hx_vm.c HX_SLOT_PEPPER) on 2026-09-02.

entries.expr_note: the construction upstream states for mdxfind type SHA1-MD5PEPPER-MD5MD5SALT (e611) uses a PEPPER: a site-wide secret that appears in no hash and cannot be derived from one. hx makes it a built-in variable beside pass, salt and salt2, with its own slot in the VM, and mdxfind reads it from a file (-j global array, -P per-type). john's dynamic expression language has no equivalent: $s2 is a second PER-HASH salt, not a site secret, and a $c1 constant would have to carry the value, which is exactly what a pepper does not publish. The absence therefore holds for every possible pepper rather than for this vector, which is what makes it a lookup. It says nothing about whether john can CRACK this. Established from mdxfind's source (hx.y line 19, hx_vm.c HX_SLOT_PEPPER) on 2026-09-02.

entries.expr_note: the construction upstream states for mdxfind type SHA1-PEPPER-MD5SALT (e677) uses a PEPPER: a site-wide secret that appears in no hash and cannot be derived from one. hx makes it a built-in variable beside pass, salt and salt2, with its own slot in the VM, and mdxfind reads it from a file (-j global array, -P per-type). john's dynamic expression language has no equivalent: $s2 is a second PER-HASH salt, not a site secret, and a $c1 constant would have to carry the value, which is exactly what a pepper does not publish. The absence therefore holds for every possible pepper rather than for this vector, which is what makes it a lookup. It says nothing about whether john can CRACK this. entries.expr_note: CORRECTED 2026-09-02. This row previously carried sha1($p), on the reading that dynamic_1023 truncates the STORAGE and the expression describes the computation. Withdrawn for one reason: the expression is this repository join key, and axcryptsha1 (mdxfind e916) already spells the identical construction as cut(sha1($p),0,32). Two rows for one computation that spell it differently do not join, which is the entire point of the field. The cut is also what this row own name, its legacy hashes_org name CUT0-32SHA1, and john own --list=subformats all say: john states dynamic_1023 as "sha1($p) (hash truncated to length 32)", for an identifier this row proved by round-trip. mdxfind hx VM, built -DHX_STANDALONE 2026-09-02, evaluates cut(sha1(pass),0,32) to d21af7ece046af0e12d3c38472792cd5, this row first vector, exactly. Tier stays upstream and cannot become vector: cut() has no john dynamic spelling at all (RosettaJohn %NO_JOHN), so john compiler can never be handed this string, and john_dynamic_expr has been WITHDRAWN for the same reason -- the dynamic=sha1($p) it used to carry runs happily and produces the 40-hex digest, not the 32-hex ciphertext stored here. CAVEAT, unresolved and left for a curator: this row second vector is the FULL 40-hex sha1("rosetta") and does not satisfy this expression, and hashcat -m 100, mdxfind SHA1, john dynamic_26 and raw-SHA1-opencl are all plain-SHA1 identifiers that compute no cut. See the curation note in notes:.; TRIAGE 2026-09-08 [compiler-cannot]: the expression is correct -- computed here with Digest:: it reproduces all 6 of john's own test vectors for dynamic_1023 -- and john's ad-hoc compiler still recovers none of them, so the string is right and --format=dynamic cannot execute it

entries.notes: RESOLVED 2026-09-04 by Royce, and the reasoning is kept because the shape recurs. This row was being asked to be two computations: its expression is cut(sha1($p),0,32), its 32-hex vector satisfies it, and the 40-hex sha1("rosetta") it also carried did not. Only john's dynamic_1023 truncates; the other five identifiers computed plain SHA-1. relations.note: Both compute cut(sha1(pass),0,32); mdxfind hx VM reproduces each row own vector from that one string, 2026-09-02. They stay separate rows because the ciphertext SERIALIZATION differs: AxCrypt stores it behind a $axcrypt_sha1$ prefix and hashcat gives that its own mode 13300, where this row stores the bare 32 hex characters. Same computation, two encodings, two identifiers a reader can arrive by.

This row is sha1 cut to its first 32 hex characters. RESOLVED 2026-09-04 by Royce: the plain-SHA-1 identifiers this row carried -- hashcat 100, mdxfind SHA1, hashpipe SHA1, john dynamic_26 and raw-SHA1-opencl -- compute no cut and moved to the new sha1 row with the 40-hex vector they were proven against. Note what is NOT a mapping: mdxfind's SHA1 and hashpipe's SHA1 do recover the 32-hex vector, because mdxfind compares at the length of the shortest hash it loaded and cracking a truncated digest is a capability it has by design. That is the tool being able to crack this, not the tool having an identifier for the truncation, and "mdxfind -h '^SHA1$'" is still the command for it. mdxfind reproduces this row under BOTH SHA1 (e8) and AICH (e21), pinned, through its generic truncated matching at a comparison width of 32. NO mdxfind mapping is recorded: decided by Royce 2026-09-07 that finding a row is not denoting it. MD5 was pinned in the same run and REFUSED, which is the control that says the match is about these types and not about mdxfind reading a short digest loosely.

entries.expr_note: Established from mdxfind's own source and a measurement, not from a document: Appendix A writes only the prose "(complex: iterates over single-char salts)" for this family and Note [24] does not name it. mdxfind.c sweeps a single salt byte over 9 and 32..126 -- 96 values -- and emits five placements at each (s.d, d.s, s.d.s, s.s.d and d.s.s, where d is the hex inner digest); "mdxfind -z" prints 480 candidates per password, which is 5 x 96. Measured 2026-09-02 against RCS 1.545. The name and aliases on this entry are those five placements. mdxfind type SHA11SALTMD5SHA256 (e763) is MULTI-EMIT: it computes several candidate digests per input and matches if any one reproduces the stored hash. There is therefore no single expression to record, and writing one of the emitted forms into expression: would be a false claim even though the string itself is correct. This is also why two vectors of such a type can disagree with each other, and why a tool matching one of them is not evidence about the other.
entries.name: SHA11SALTMD5SHA256

relations.note: AICH of a single block is SHA-1, and SHA1lsb35 is SHA-1 with the leading nibbles masked to zero, so any tool that ignores that field -- hashcat -m 100 skips positions 0-7 and john Raw-SHA1-Linkedin skips 0-4, measured 2026-09-01, and the mask is 5 nibbles wide -- reports one for the other. They agree on every input outside those nibbles and differ nowhere else that such a tool looks.

SHA1UC is SHA-1 written in uppercase hex and SHA1lsb35 is SHA-1 with the leading nibbles masked to zero, so a tool that skips that field cannot tell them apart: hashcat -m 100 skips hash positions 0-7 and john Raw-SHA1-Linkedin skips 0-4, measured 2026-09-01. SHA1lsb35 masks exactly 5 nibbles, so either blind spot covers the whole difference: the digests are identical from position 5 onward.

entries.expr_note: mdxfind type SHA1MD5HUM (e364) is MULTI-EMIT: it computes several candidate digests per input and matches if any one reproduces the stored hash. There is therefore no single expression to record, and writing one of the emitted forms into expression: would be a false claim even though the string itself is correct. This is also why two vectors of such a type can disagree with each other, and why a tool matching one of them is not evidence about the other.

entries.expr_note: the construction upstream states for mdxfind type SHA1MD5SALTPASSPEPPER (e607) uses a PEPPER: a site-wide secret that appears in no hash and cannot be derived from one. hx makes it a built-in variable beside pass, salt and salt2, with its own slot in the VM, and mdxfind reads it from a file (-j global array, -P per-type). john's dynamic expression language has no equivalent: $s2 is a second PER-HASH salt, not a site secret, and a $c1 constant would have to carry the value, which is exactly what a pepper does not publish. The absence therefore holds for every possible pepper rather than for this vector, which is what makes it a lookup. It says nothing about whether john can CRACK this. Established from mdxfind's source (hx.y line 19, hx_vm.c HX_SLOT_PEPPER) on 2026-09-02.
entries.name: SHA1MD5SALTPASSPEPPER
entries.notes: The vector here is NOT the one mdxfind's published catalog carries. mdxfind 1.543 (2026-08-29) changed what e607 computes: the old code staged the inner digest at linebuf+saltlen while writing the pepper at a fixed offset 32, so for any non-empty salt the hash covered the salt, then a TRUNCATED digest, then the pepper, and the output depended on the salt length. dlr's own note says any hash cracked as e607 before that revision will not verify against it. The catalog example 786aab530907a783e9c25a2c7326ab7907ebf798 is the PRE-FIX digest and was still being published on 2026-09-02, so it is upstream's stale artefact rather than a vector this row should carry. Replaced 2026-09-02 with the repaired construction sha1(md5(salt . pass) . pepper), established three independent ways: the source at RCS 1.545, a Digest:: recomputation in perl that reproduces 786aab... under the old layout and 0992047f... under the new, and the rebuilt binary cracking 0992047f... The salt field holds SALT then PEPPER, space separated, both 1122334455667788 here; a pepper is a site-wide secret that appears in no hash, so mdxfind reads it from a file (-j).

entries.name: SHA1SALTCX
entries.notes: This row has NO vector and that is a deliberate withholding, measured 2026-09-04. The only example anyone publishes for this type -- mdxfind's own inventory row and the vendored hashpipe catalog carry the same string -- b59b77c52921e5df0d007fec2518e0f726ce3aaf:administrator:password123, is a TEN-ITERATION hash, and this row declares no iteration count, which the schema reads as one. Both oracles agree and each refuses the wrong depth: hashpipe -c asked for SHA1SALTCXx01 refuses and emits SHA1SALTCXx10 when asked bare, and mdxfind -h '^SHA1SALTCX$' -i 1 finds nothing while -i 10 reproduces the line exactly, as SHA1SALTCXx10. Storing it here would put an x10 digest under an x01 row, which is the defect audit-iterations.pl exists to catch -- the iteration suffix is identity, not a tuning knob. The type does support depth 1 (hashpipe's source notes it verifies at every depth, x01 included); nobody has published a depth-1 example, and one generated locally could not promote mdxfind anyway. So this needs a curator: either a depth-1 vector from upstream, or a decision that this row is about SHA1SALTCXx10 and should say so. Worth reporting upstream: the catalog publishes a depth-10 example with nothing in the row to say the depth is not 1.

entries.denotation: SHA1SHA256CAP is MULTI-EMIT: it emits sha1() of the inner sha256 hex digest, sweeping which lower-case hex characters of that digest are upper-cased. The number of emissions varies with the digest; it was 27 for "rosetta".
entries.expr_note: WITHDRAWN 2026-09-02. This row carried sha1(cap(sha256($p))) at tier upstream, transcribed from hx Appendix A for e632. It is ONE of 27 forms and so a false claim on its own: mdxfind type SHA1SHA256CAP is MULTI-EMIT, sweeping which characters of the inner sha256 digest are upper-cased in the same way JOB_SHA1SHA11CAP does. A full sweep of all 1002 types with mdxfind -z measured 27 on 2026-09-02 against RCS 1.545 -- more than SHA1SHA11CAP because a sha256 digest is 64 hex characters and so carries more lower-case letters, which is the input-dependence itself. No single expression can describe that.

relations.note: SHA1UC is SHA-1 written in uppercase hex and SHA1lsb35 is SHA-1 with the leading nibbles masked to zero, so a tool that skips that field cannot tell them apart: hashcat -m 100 skips hash positions 0-7 and john Raw-SHA1-Linkedin skips 0-4, measured 2026-09-01. SHA1lsb35 masks exactly 5 nibbles, so either blind spot covers the whole difference: the digests are identical from position 5 onward.

tool_note.hashcat: proven three ways because -m 100 alone is not enough: hashcat cracked this row's own vector under mode 100, john's Raw-SHA1 and dynamic_26 cracked it too with a FULL digest comparison, and Digest::SHA confirms sha1("password123") is cbfdac6008f9cab4083784cbd1874f76618d2a97 character for character. The third step is required here: measured 2026-08-31, hashcat -m 100 skips hash positions 0-7, so on its own it cannot tell this row from sha1lsb35, which is the same digest with those nibbles masked. discover-hashcat.pl's canary withheld the claim for exactly that reason; this is a human overriding it with the independent recomputation, not the tool's word.
tool_note.hashpipe: verified by round-tripping each type PINNED with -m, not by taking an unpinned report: hashpipe names the FIRST type that reproduces a digest, so an unpinned answer names a type that works and not necessarily this one.
tool_note.john: format discovered by round-trip search, not by name. Raw-SHA1-Linkedin was recorded here by discover-john.pl on 2026-08-31 and WITHDRAWN the same day. It is john's format for the LinkedIn leak, whose hashes have their leading nibbles zeroed, and it ignores hash positions 0-4 -- the 20 bits that leak zeroed -- measured position by position on 2026-09-01. That is the same defect the hashcat canary found in -m 100, at a different width: -m 100 skips 0-7. It therefore cracks any full SHA-1 digest as well, which is a collision and not a denotation. Raw-SHA1 and dynamic_26 both compare the whole digest and were re-checked position by position.
tool_note.mdxfind: NOT REPRODUCED HERE. mdxfind publishes this identifier and a worked example, which is what tier `upstream` means, but the local round-trip FAILED: the tool pinned to this identifier did not reproduce its own published example. The row exists so that someone arriving by this identifier is not met with nothing; the claim is upstream's, not this repository's, until a vector is round-tripped here. Re-run seed-orphans.pl --tool mdxfind --only SHA1UC to retry.

entries.expr_note: mdxfind type SHA256HEXSALT (e185) is MULTI-EMIT: it computes several candidate digests per input and matches if any one reproduces the stored hash. There is therefore no single expression to record, and writing one of the emitted forms into expression: would be a false claim even though the string itself is correct. This is also why two vectors of such a type can disagree with each other, and why a tool matching one of them is not evidence about the other.

entries.name: sha512($pass.$salt)

relations.note: Both mdxfind types reproduce BOTH entries' vectors at x01, measured 2026-09-05 with hashpipe -c pinned to each in turn: SHA512RAWPASSSALT and SHA512PASSSALT agree on every input at one iteration, because at depth 1 the only difference between them is whether the digest is emitted as raw bytes or as hex, and the stored form is hex either way. They are NOT the same computation, and depth 2 shows it: SHA512RAWPASSSALTx02 verifies sha512(sha512_raw($p.$s)) = e785d2e3... while SHA512PASSSALTx02 verifies sha512(sha512_hex($p.$s)) = 3de674ce..., for the same password123/DB1C19C0. So this is a coincidence on the x01 subset, which is every input this repository stores, and not an equivalence. It is also why john's dynamic_82 cracks sha512rawpasssalt's vector and is deliberately NOT recorded as a mapping there: per CLAUDE.md, record the trap, not the mapping.

Both rows are one computation, and each exists because a tool publishes a separate identifier for it: hashcat 15000 "FileZilla Server >= 0.9.55" against hashcat 1710 "sha512($pass.$salt)". PROVEN RATHER THAN INFERRED, 2026-09-08: mdxfind pinned to ^SHA512PASSSALT$ reproduced every member of this cluster from its OWN stored vector, against the local build RCS 1.579. A shared type name alone would not have established it -- mdxfind's EPISERVER reproduces a SHA-1 row and a SHA-256 row because the string carries a variant tag it dispatches on -- so the second control is that every digest in this cluster is 128 characters wide, which leaves the type no variant field to have read.

relations.note: Both mdxfind types reproduce BOTH entries' vectors at x01, measured 2026-09-05 with hashpipe -c pinned to each in turn: SHA512RAWPASSSALT and SHA512PASSSALT agree on every input at one iteration, because at depth 1 the only difference between them is whether the digest is emitted as raw bytes or as hex, and the stored form is hex either way. They are NOT the same computation, and depth 2 shows it: SHA512RAWPASSSALTx02 verifies sha512(sha512_raw($p.$s)) = e785d2e3... while SHA512PASSSALTx02 verifies sha512(sha512_hex($p.$s)) = 3de674ce..., for the same password123/DB1C19C0. So this is a coincidence on the x01 subset, which is every input this repository stores, and not an equivalence. It is also why john's dynamic_82 cracks sha512rawpasssalt's vector and is deliberately NOT recorded as a mapping there: per CLAUDE.md, record the trap, not the mapping.

The plaintext is john's finding, not the source's claim: each hash was cracked under the CPU format this entry names and under the GPU build that has no CPU twin, and both recovered the plaintext recorded here.

tool_note.john: Round-tripped here on 2026-09-01, under both tc_ripemd160 and TrueCrypt-opencl, against both vectors this entry carries. It had been tier upstream with a note saying the local round trip FAILED; the real obstacle was that john --list=format-details truncates example_ciphertext at 896 characters, so the volume header in data/tools/john.yaml is not a loadable hash. The vectors here come from john's own src/opencl_tc_fmt_plug.c test array, and john found their plaintexts -- see notes:. GPU build TrueCrypt-opencl has no CPU format of that name, so discover-john.pl --mirror-gpu could not place it; tools/probe-gpu.pl proved it.

tool_note.john: dynamic_6 and dynamic_1007 were REMOVED 2026-09-06. Both compute this row's construction and neither is wrong about it; neither can LOAD this row's vector. john caps their salt at 23 bytes, and a vBulletin salt from 3.8.5 on is 30, which is the whole reason john ships dynamic_2006 -- its own subformat listing calls it "md5(md5($p).$s) (vBulletin, PW > 55 bytes or/and salt > 23 bytes)". Measured 2026-09-06 with the vector spelled $dynamic_N$<hash>$<salt> so that the parser could not be the variable: dynamic_6 and dynamic_1007 do not load it at all, dynamic_2006 loads and cracks it, and the control -- john's own 6-byte-salt example -- falls to dynamic_6 on the first try. They keep their proof on vbulletin-v3-8-5, the short-salt row, where all three are tier vector.

entries.name: WPA-EAPOL

relations.note: hashcat 22000 "WPA-PBKDF2-PMKID+EAPOL" accepts EITHER artifact -- a PMKID or an EAPOL handshake -- where wpa-eapol carries one of the two. So this is NOT same-computation: for a given input the two agree exactly, and the covering identifier additionally accepts inputs the other does not. hashcat's own mode name states the union, so unlike a row that overstates its own scope, this row names its identifier faithfully and no merge is owed. 'covers' was added to the vocabulary on 2026-09-08 for exactly this, decided by Royce: same-computation overstates it and collides-on-subset means the opposite thing. Measured 2026-09-08, not read off the two names. The corpus holds three WPA serializations, one per generation of tooling -- hashcat's hccapx (2500/2501), its pmkid line (16800/16801) and the WPA*NN* form -- and no sweep had ever related these rows because each tool is silent about another tool's spelling, which is not evidence. tmp/wpa-canon.pl converts all three to WPA*NN*, checking hccapx's HCPX magic first because every field after it is positional. 2500 and 2501 turn out to carry the IDENTICAL blob, and 16800/16801 the identical PMKID and MACs: each pair is one credential asked two ways. Every claim here is a round trip against hashcat v7.1.2-606 and mdxfind RCS 1.579, each with a WRONGCANDIDATE control that found nothing.

One computation under two tools' names: mdxfind WPA-EAPOL and hashcat 2500 (WPA-EAPOL-PBKDF2). Both rows' own credentials were reproduced by a SINGLE identifier, which is what makes this same-computation rather than a resemblance. Measured 2026-09-08, not read off the two names. The corpus holds three WPA serializations, one per generation of tooling -- hashcat's hccapx (2500/2501), its pmkid line (16800/16801) and the WPA*NN* form -- and no sweep had ever related these rows because each tool is silent about another tool's spelling, which is not evidence. tmp/wpa-canon.pl converts all three to WPA*NN*, checking hccapx's HCPX magic first because every field after it is positional. 2500 and 2501 turn out to carry the IDENTICAL blob, and 16800/16801 the identical PMKID and MACs: each pair is one credential asked two ways. Every claim here is a round trip against hashcat v7.1.2-606 and mdxfind RCS 1.579, each with a WRONGCANDIDATE control that found nothing. One trap is worth carrying: the first EAPOL conversion produced a line nothing would crack, and "wrong conversion" and "these rows differ" are indistinguishable from that alone. The EAPOL frame's key-info word is 0x0109 -- MIC set, ACK clear -- so the frame is M2 and carries the STA's nonce, and that value equalled the field hccap.h NAMES nonce_ap. The SECOND 32-byte nonce field is the one hashcat's WPA*02* slot wants, in both hccap_t and hccapx_t; the header comments are not a guide. The two rows also store their vectors in different serializations, but that is not WHY both exist: each row is where a reader arrives from a different tool's identifier, which is what distinction 'naming' means.
